## Global Instructions

### Dart and Flutter MCP

Before the first Dart MCP call in a session, call `roots` (`command: add`) with the workspace `file://` URI.

Prefer Dart MCP over text search for Dart code:

- declarations: `lsp` `resolveWorkspaceSymbol` with the exact full name (matching is fuzzy and includes dependencies and the SDK);
- types, docs, call parameters: `lsp` `hover` or `signatureHelp` (positions are zero-based);
- pub dependency sources: `read_package_uris`, `rip_grep_packages`;
- diagnostics for specific files: `analyze_files`.

Use text search for usages and implementations; `lsp` cannot find them.

After changing Dart code, look for a running app via `dtd`. If one exists, hot reload or restart it and check `get_runtime_errors`; otherwise run the repository's CLI checks.

### Language preferences

Use Russian by default for all text in this repository and for communication with the user.

IMPORTANT: Russian is mandatory for:

- Communication with the user.
- Human-facing documents: PRDs, task documents, specifications, research notes, project guides, journals, and public text, even when agents also read them.
- Code comments.
- Test names and test descriptions.

Use English only for text intended exclusively for agents, including agent instructions and skills. Agents handle English more reliably, and it usually uses fewer tokens.

Continue existing English-language documents in English for consistency.

### Responsible testing

A test is a cost until it earns its place: it adds runtime, review effort, and friction to every future refactor. Write a test only when its absence would let a plausible, costly regression go unnoticed. Coverage, symmetry with neighboring tests, and the existence of a spec scenario are not reasons on their own. Before adding a test, name the regression it catches; if you cannot, do not write it.

#### Test behavior, not state

- Drive the code through its public interface — user actions, public API, repository contract — and assert what a user or consumer can observe: visible text and semantics, persisted and read data, returned results and failures.
- Do not assert widget keys or tree shape, pixel geometry without a stated layout requirement, object identity, internal fields of view-model or snapshot state, revision, epoch, or claim tokens, call counts or order, SQL text, or statement counts.
- A test that breaks on a behavior-preserving refactor checks implementation. Rewrite it against behavior, or delete it when the behavior is covered elsewhere; do not adjust it to the new internals.

#### Test each behavior once

- Test a behavior at the cheapest level where it is observable. Do not repeat a scenario across view-model, page, and app tests; add a higher-level test only for wiring that lower levels cannot show, and keep one end-to-end path per user flow.
- Test a shared mechanism — diagnostics sink, command coordinator, shared widget, error classifier — once at its own boundary, not again at every call site or for every command kind.
- Prove durability, crash safety, and rollback once per storage mechanism, not once per operation.
- A spec scenario needs one test that shows it, not one per layer.

#### Do not write tests that

- Restate what the compiler, the language, or a framework guarantees: constructors, getters, equality, `hashCode`, `toString`, sealed or enum exhaustiveness, unmodifiable collections, constants.
- Exercise fakes, fixtures, or test helpers instead of product code.
- Build states the product cannot reach, such as rows written with schema constraints disabled or a repository breaking its own contract. When such a state is real, for example on-disk corruption, test recovery from it once.
- Enumerate combinatorial matrices — locale, text scale, screen size, timing, failure point — whose dimensions do not change the code path. Pick representative cases: the default, the boundary, and the case that actually differs.
- Chase race or timing orders that the architecture already rules out, for example commands serialized by one executor.
- Measure performance without asserting a threshold. When a cost requirement exists, assert the user-relevant bound, such as page size or a time budget, not the query shape.

This rule decides what to test; `test-driven-development` decides how. Its red-green-refactor cycle applies to tests that pass this rule, and this rule overrides that skill's advice to test simple code because it may grow complicated.

### Spec first

Application behavior changes only through an active spec change under `openspec/changes/`. Write the spec change first, then the product code that implements it. Product code that changes behavior without a driving spec change is invalid, even if all tests pass.

No spec change is required for work that leaves application behavior unchanged, such as:

- CI workflows, build and repository configuration;
- local developer tooling and scripts;
- tests, comments, and documentation;
- behavior-preserving refactoring.

When it is unclear whether a change alters application behavior, treat it as behavior-changing.

If behavior-changing product code exists without a driving spec change, especially when acceptance tests fail, discard the code and restart from the spec. Patching unspecced code until tests pass is a rule violation, not a fix.

### Type-safe design

Prefer designs that make invalid states unrepresentable and let the compiler enforce invariants. Where practical, use precise types, enums, sealed variants, generics, and exhaustive handling instead of runtime type checks, stringly typed values, unchecked casts, or condition-heavy validation.

Validate untrusted data at system boundaries, then convert it into trusted, type-safe domain types. Accept runtime checks or a less strict design only when stronger static guarantees would add disproportionate complexity.

### Commit message conventions

When generating Git commit messages, use Conventional Commits.

Format:

<type>(<scope>): <description>

Allowed types:

- feat
- fix
- refactor
- test
- docs
- chore
- build
- ci
- perf
- style

Rules:

- Write all commit messages in English.
- Infer scope from changed files.
- Keep subject under 72 characters.
- Use the concise imperative mood.
- Do not use vague messages like "update files" or "misc changes".

### Domain language

When a domain model exists, use the canonical terms from the relevant `CONTEXT.md` in all communication and project work. If `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists, use it to select the applicable glossary. Explicitly resolve any terminology conflicts before proceeding.

### Process discipline

Reaching the expected result is not enough; reach it through the process the repository expects. A result reached by an improvised process is hard to review and repeat, and usually drops constraints the process exists to protect.

#### Read the skills that apply

- When a skill available in the current context clearly covers the situation, read it in full, with the resources it points to, before the first action it governs.
- Treat a description as routing only. It carries none of the skill's constraints, formats, ordering, decision criteria, or failure handling.
- A skill is present because default behavior was judged insufficient. Assume it encodes details you cannot infer, and do not let familiarity with the topic replace reading it.
- Read each skill that governs a distinct part of the work, and resolve conflicts between them explicitly.
- Do not use every available skill. A loosely related skill only adds noise; the obligation covers an unmistakable match.

#### Follow OpenSpec instructions

- When a repository uses OpenSpec, its instructions, schema, and templates are deliberate human decisions about the path to a result, not reference material for after the fact.
- Read them before creating or changing an artifact, and follow their stages, structure, and syntax.
- Validate with the project's tooling, such as `openspec validate`.
- Do not skip, reorder, or compress stages because you expect the same outcome without them.
- Deviate only when a human directs it or an instruction cannot be satisfied, and state what you deviated from and why.

### Production readiness

Build every feature to production-ready standards from its first implementation.

Do not use labels such as MVP, prototype, test release, or initial version to justify deferring essential engineering work. Every delivered capability must include an appropriate level of:

- correctness;
- reliability;
- security;
- maintainability;
- observability;
- test coverage;
- failure handling.

When time or resources constrain delivery, reduce the number of capabilities in scope. Do not lower the engineering quality of the capabilities that remain.
